textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Foundations of Healthcare Economics
prompt: Write a comprehensive introductory chapter for graduate-level health economics researchers and health services researchers. Cover: (1) the unique economic properties of healthcare as a commodity — Arrow's 1963 seminal paper and its enduring implications, uncertainty, asymmetric information, agency relationships, moral hazard, adverse selection; (2) the healthcare production function — Grossman's 1972 human capital model of health demand, health as both a consumption good and an investment good, depreciation of health stock; (3) market failures in healthcare — externalities (vaccination, antibiotic resistance), public goods characteristics of medical knowledge, non-competitive market structures, information asymmetry between providers and patients; (4) the three fundamental questions of health economics: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom; (5) welfare economics foundations — Pareto efficiency, Kaldor-Hicks compensation, the two fundamental theorems of welfare economics applied to healthcare; (6) the economic case for government intervention — regulatory approaches, public provision, financing mechanisms; (7) a taxonomy of health economics research: positive vs. normative, micro vs. macro, demand-side vs. supply-side analysis. Engage with foundational literature: Arrow (1963), Grossman (1972), Pauly (1968), Akerlof (1970), Rothschild-Stiglitz (1976). This chapter must set the intellectual framework that all subsequent chapters build upon.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Healthcare Demand: Theory and Empirical Evidence
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter targeting graduate health economics researchers on the theory and empirics of healthcare demand. Cover: (1) consumer theory applied to healthcare — utility maximization subject to budget constraints, the demand for health vs. the demand for medical care (Grossman model revisited), derived demand for healthcare inputs; (2) price elasticity of demand for healthcare — the RAND Health Insurance Experiment (Manning et al., 1987) as the landmark study, its experimental design, key findings, criticisms, and lasting policy influence; (3) the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment (Finkelstein et al., 2012) and what it revealed about Medicaid coverage effects on utilization, health outcomes, and financial protection; (4) moral hazard in health insurance — ex-ante and ex-post moral hazard, empirical evidence on behavioral responses to insurance coverage, the welfare economics of moral hazard (Pauly 1968 vs. Nyman 2003 access value theory); (5) demand for preventive care vs. acute care — differential price sensitivity, evidence from behavioral economics interventions; (6) physician-induced demand — theoretical models (McGuire 2000), empirical evidence for and against, endogeneity challenges in testing the hypothesis; (7) time costs and non-monetary barriers to healthcare access — travel time, wait time, opportunity costs, their differential impact across socioeconomic groups; (8) behavioral economics and healthcare demand — bounded rationality, present bias, framing effects, nudges in health insurance choice and medication adherence. Include at least two worked demand estimation examples with mathematical derivations.
context_summary: Chapter 1 established the foundational economic properties of healthcare (Arrow, Grossman, moral hazard, adverse selection, market failures). Assume the reader knows these concepts. This chapter goes deep into the demand side.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Healthcare Supply: Provider Behavior and Market Structure
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter for graduate health economics researchers on the supply side of healthcare. Cover: (1) physician labor supply — human capital investment in medical training, specialty choice as economic decision-making, geographic distribution of physicians and market incentive explanations, the physician supply curve and its peculiarities; (2) hospital as an economic firm — not-for-profit vs. for-profit hospital behavior, Newhouse's (1970) utility-maximizing model, Lakdawalla-Philipson (2006) competition model, empirical evidence on quality and cost differences by ownership type; (3) hospital market concentration and competition — Herfindahl-Hirschman Index applications, merger analysis, the competition-quality relationship (Kessler-McClellan 2000, Gaynor-Town 2012), price effects of hospital consolidation; (4) provider payment mechanisms and supply responses — fee-for-service incentives, capitation, bundled payments, pay-for-performance, the target income hypothesis for physicians; (5) the production of health services — technical efficiency vs. allocative efficiency, stochastic frontier analysis concepts, Data Envelopment Analysis basics; (6) the pharmaceutical industry — R&D investment under patent protection, generic entry, pricing strategies, the role of pharmacy benefit managers; (7) the healthcare workforce beyond physicians — nursing supply, advanced practice providers, team-based care production functions, substitution and complementarity among healthcare workers; (8) vertical and horizontal integration in healthcare — economics of physician-hospital integration, accountable care organizations as organizational innovations. Include theoretical models with mathematical notation and reference landmark empirical studies throughout.
context_summary: Chapters 1-2 covered foundations and healthcare demand (Arrow, Grossman, RAND HIE, Oregon experiment, moral hazard, behavioral economics). This chapter addresses the supply side and market structure.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Health Insurance Economics and Market Design
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on health insurance economics for graduate researchers. Cover: (1) the economic theory of insurance — expected utility theory, risk aversion, certainty equivalents, the demand for insurance (Rothschild-Stiglitz 1976), optimal insurance contracts under symmetric and asymmetric information; (2) adverse selection in health insurance markets — theoretical models (Akerlof 1970 applied to insurance), Cutler-Zeckhauser (1998) evidence, death spiral dynamics, Einav-Finkelstein-Cullen (2010) sufficient statistics approach to welfare analysis of selection; (3) moral hazard — static and dynamic models, the optimal insurance design problem balancing risk protection against moral hazard costs, arc vs. point elasticity debates; (4) US health insurance market structure — employer-sponsored insurance (ESI) and the tax subsidy, individual markets, Medicare (Parts A/B/C/D structure, payment systems, quality programs), Medicaid (federal-state structure, expansion under ACA), VA system; (5) the Affordable Care Act — economic analysis of key provisions (individual mandate, essential health benefits, risk corridors/reinsurance/risk adjustment, exchanges, Medicaid expansion), pre-post evidence on coverage, utilization, and health outcomes; (6) managed care — HMO/PPO/POS models, selective contracting, utilization management, capitation vs. fee-for-service incentive alignment, the managed care backlash and its economic interpretation; (7) value-based insurance design — tiered formularies, reference pricing, high-deductible health plans with HSAs, evidence on effects; (8) international comparison of insurance system architectures — Beveridge vs. Bismarck vs. national health insurance vs. out-of-pocket systems, single-payer economic arguments. Include mathematical derivations of optimal insurance and adverse selection equilibria.
context_summary: Chapters 1-3 established foundations, demand theory (RAND HIE, Oregon experiment), and supply-side economics. Insurance was introduced conceptually. This chapter provides the full insurance economics treatment.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Healthcare Financing and Payment Systems
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter for graduate researchers on healthcare financing and payment system design. Cover: (1) national health expenditure accounting — the CMS NHE framework, sources of financing (public vs. private, federal vs. state/local), categories of spending, international comparison using OECD SHA methodology, trends and projections; (2) provider payment mechanisms — fee-for-service (CPT/HCPCS coding, RBRVS, conversion factors, the SGR formula history), prospective payment (DRG system design, MS-DRG refinements, outlier payments, CMI calculation), capitation (full vs. partial, risk adjustment methods, withhold and surplus sharing), bundled payments (BPCI, CJR model design and evaluation); (3) value-based payment — pay-for-performance (Premier HQID, Hospital VBP Program, MIPS), shared savings (MSSP design, benchmark methodology, quality gates), episode-based payment, global budgets (Maryland All-Payer Model); (4) risk adjustment in payment systems — Hierarchical Condition Categories (HCC), CMS-HCC model structure, concurrent vs. prospective risk adjustment, gaming and upcoding concerns, DxCG and ACG systems; (5) physician compensation models — productivity-based (wRVU), salary, blended models, the shift toward value-based physician compensation; (6) healthcare cost drivers — Baumol's cost disease, technology diffusion, administrative costs (Woolhandler-Himmelstein research), prices vs. utilization decomposition; (7) cost containment strategies — supply-side (certificate of need, rate setting, global budgets) vs. demand-side (cost sharing, managed care) approaches, evidence on effectiveness; (8) the economics of healthcare price transparency — reference pricing, surprise billing legislation, all-payer claims databases. Ground every section in the USA context with specific payment model details and CMS program mechanics.
context_summary: Chapters 1-4 covered foundations, demand, supply, and insurance economics. This chapter addresses how money flows through the healthcare system — financing sources and provider payment mechanisms.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Cost-Effectiveness Analysis and Health Technology Assessment
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter for graduate health economics researchers on economic evaluation methods for healthcare interventions. Cover: (1) types of economic evaluation — cost-minimization analysis (CMA), cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA), cost-utility analysis (CUA), cost-benefit analysis (CBA), their appropriate uses, strengths, and limitations; (2) measuring costs — perspective choice (societal, healthcare sector, payer), micro-costing vs. gross-costing, time horizon, discounting (rates and rationale), handling inflation and currency conversion; (3) measuring health outcomes — quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) including utility elicitation methods (standard gamble, time trade-off, EQ-5D, SF-6D, HUI), disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and the Global Burden of Disease methodology, years of life saved, disease-specific outcome measures; (4) the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) — calculation, interpretation, the cost-effectiveness plane, dominance and extended dominance, the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve (CEAC); (5) willingness-to-pay thresholds — $50K-$150K/QALY in the USA, NICE threshold in England, the empirical basis (or lack thereof) for threshold values, Neumann et al. recommendations; (6) decision-analytic modeling — decision trees, Markov models, microsimulation, discrete event simulation, model validation and calibration; (7) sensitivity analysis — one-way, multi-way, probabilistic sensitivity analysis (Monte Carlo simulation), value of information analysis (EVPI, EVPPI), expected value of sample information (EVSI); (8) budget impact analysis — purpose, methods, relationship to CEA; (9) the Second Panel on Cost-Effectiveness in Health and Medicine (Sanders et al., 2016) recommendations; (10) real-world applications — walk through a complete CEA example from problem framing through ICER calculation to sensitivity analysis. Include mathematical formulations of QALY calculation, Markov transition probabilities, and PSA methodology.
context_summary: Chapters 1-5 covered microeconomic foundations, demand/supply, insurance, and financing. This chapter introduces the primary economic evaluation toolkit used to assess whether healthcare interventions represent good value.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Healthcare Quality Measurement and Value
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter for graduate researchers on the economics of healthcare quality measurement and the value equation. Cover: (1) defining and measuring quality — Donabedian's structure-process-outcome framework, IOM's six aims (STEEEP), the relationship between quality measurement and economic incentives; (2) quality measurement infrastructure — NQF endorsement process, CMS quality programs (Hospital Compare, Star Ratings, HEDIS), AHRQ Quality Indicators (PSIs, IQIs, PDIs), risk adjustment for quality comparison (observed-to-expected ratios, hierarchical models); (3) the economics of medical errors — IOM 'To Err Is Human' economic estimates, the cost of adverse events, never events and non-payment policies, economics of patient safety interventions; (4) pay-for-performance economics — theoretical models of P4P optimal design (Mullen et al. 2010), empirical evidence from Hospital VBP, Premier HQID, UK QOF, evidence on gaming and teaching to the test; (5) public reporting and information economics — theoretical effects on provider behavior and consumer choice, empirical evidence on whether patients use quality information, the role of information asymmetry reduction; (6) value-based healthcare frameworks — Porter's value equation (outcomes/cost), triple aim and quadruple aim, alternative payment models as value-alignment mechanisms; (7) disparities in healthcare quality — economic determinants of quality disparities by race, income, geography, rurality; (8) the cost of poor quality — waste taxonomy (Berwick and Hackbarth 2012), overuse economics, low-value care identification and measurement (Choosing Wisely), the economics of defensive medicine. Ground discussion in USA-specific quality programs, measurement systems, and regulatory frameworks.
context_summary: Chapters 1-6 covered foundations through cost-effectiveness analysis. Quality and value are the bridge between clinical outcomes and economic analysis. This chapter provides the measurement and incentive framework.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Rural Health Economics and Critical Access Hospitals
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter for graduate researchers on the economics of rural healthcare delivery, with emphasis on Critical Access Hospital (CAH) viability and rural health policy. Cover: (1) defining rural — census-based definitions, RUCA codes, FORHP designations, OMB metro/micro classifications, why definition matters for policy and research; (2) the rural health economic model — lower patient volumes, higher per-unit costs, payer mix challenges (higher Medicare/Medicaid share), distance and transportation costs, limited labor markets for specialized providers; (3) Critical Access Hospital program economics — 25-bed cap, 96-hour length of stay requirement, cost-based reimbursement mechanics (101% of reasonable costs), swing bed program economics, CAH designation criteria and conversion process, flex program; (4) rural hospital financial distress and closure — trends in rural hospital closures (170+ since 2005), Chartis/Navigant vulnerability index, economic impact of hospital closure on communities (employment, access, property values, mortality effects); (5) rural payment policies — sole community hospital designation, Medicare-dependent hospital program, low-volume adjustment, rural referral center status, wage index reclassification, Rural Emergency Hospital program (REH); (6) telehealth economics in rural settings — cost-effectiveness of telemedicine, store-and-forward vs. real-time economics, reimbursement policy evolution (pre and post COVID-19 flexibilities), broadband infrastructure as economic prerequisite; (7) rural workforce economics — recruitment and retention challenges, loan repayment programs (NHSC), J-1 visa waiver program, scope of practice policies for APPs, community health worker models; (8) rural health policy analysis — the tension between efficiency (consolidation) and access (maintaining local capacity), emergency medical services in rural areas, the economics of rural obstetric unit closures and maternity care deserts. Use USA-specific data, CMS payment mechanics, and cite the rural health research literature extensively.
context_summary: Chapters 1-7 covered healthcare economics broadly. This chapter applies those frameworks specifically to rural and Critical Access Hospital settings — a distinct economic environment with unique policy solutions.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Econometric Foundations for Health Economics Research
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter for graduate health economics researchers transitioning from economic theory to empirical methodology. Cover: (1) the identification problem in health economics — why correlation does not equal causation, the Rubin causal model (potential outcomes framework), SUTVA, the fundamental problem of causal inference, selection bias as the core challenge; (2) ordinary least squares in health economics — the classical linear model, OLS assumptions and their frequent violations in health data (heteroscedasticity, non-normal errors, measurement error), robust standard errors (Huber-White), clustered standard errors (rationale for clustering at treatment level, Bertrand-Duflo-Mullainathan 2004); (3) maximum likelihood estimation — derivation from first principles, properties (consistency, efficiency, asymptotic normality), the information matrix, likelihood ratio / Wald / LM tests, application to binary choice models; (4) generalized linear models (GLMs) in health economics — the GLM framework (link function, variance function), the Gaussian-log link for healthcare costs, the gamma distribution for right-skewed cost data, Park test for variance function selection (Manning-Mullahy 2001), modified Park test; (5) two-part models — the econometrics of zero-mass observations in healthcare data, the two-part model (hurdle model) for healthcare expenditures, comparison with Heckman selection model, smearing retransformation (Duan 1983); (6) endogeneity in health economics — omitted variable bias, simultaneity, measurement error, the direction and magnitude of bias analysis; (7) panel data fundamentals — fixed effects vs. random effects, the Hausman test, within-group estimation, first differences, correlated random effects (Mundlak approach). Include mathematical derivations and health economics examples for every estimator.
context_summary: Chapters 1-8 covered economic theory and institutional knowledge. This chapter begins the methodological half of the textbook, establishing the econometric toolkit that empirical health economists use.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Instrumental Variables and Natural Experiments in Health Economics
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on instrumental variables (IV) methods and natural experiments for graduate health economics researchers. Cover: (1) the IV framework — motivation from endogeneity, the exclusion restriction, relevance condition, the two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimator derived from first principles, the Wald estimator as the simplest IV case; (2) the local average treatment effect (LATE) — Imbens-Angrist (1994), compliers/always-takers/never-takers/defiers, monotonicity assumption, interpreting LATE vs. ATE; (3) testing instrument validity — first-stage F-statistic (Staiger-Stock rule of thumb), weak instruments problem (Stock-Wright-Yogo), Anderson-Rubin confidence sets for weak IV, over-identification tests (Sargan-Hansen J-test), falsification tests; (4) classic IV applications in health economics — distance to provider as instrument for treatment (McClellan-McNeil-Newhouse 1994 cardiac catheterization study), quarter of birth instruments (Angrist-Krueger), area variation as instrument, physician preference instruments, genetic instruments (Mendelian randomization basics); (5) natural experiments in health economics — definition and taxonomy, Medicare eligibility at age 65 (Card-Dobkin-Maestas 2008), Medicaid expansions as natural experiments, hospital market mergers, policy discontinuities; (6) fuzzy regression discontinuity as IV — the fuzzy RD-IV connection, estimation and bandwidth selection; (7) shift-share (Bartik) instruments in health economics — construction, recent econometric debates (Goldsmith-Pinkham et al. 2020, Borusyak et al. 2022), applications to healthcare labor markets and spending variation; (8) practical guidance — how to argue for instrument validity in a paper, common critiques and responses, the exclusion restriction as fundamentally untestable. Include full mathematical derivations of 2SLS and LATE, plus detailed walkthroughs of seminal health economics IV papers.
context_summary: Chapter 9 established OLS, GLM, panel data fundamentals, and the identification problem. This chapter covers the primary quasi-experimental strategy for addressing endogeneity in observational health economics data.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Difference-in-Differences and Synthetic Control Methods
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on difference-in-differences (DiD) and synthetic control methods for graduate health economics researchers. Cover: (1) the canonical 2x2 DiD — setup, the parallel trends assumption, estimation, graphical presentation, interpretation of the ATT; (2) regression-based DiD with covariates — controlling for time-varying confounders, when covariates help and when they are 'bad controls'; (3) testing and validating parallel trends — pre-treatment trend plots, event study specifications, placebo tests with fake treatment dates; (4) staggered DiD — the problem with two-way fixed effects (TWFE) when treatment timing varies, negative weighting (Goodman-Bacon 2021 decomposition, de Chaisemartin-D'Haultfoeuille 2020), heterogeneous treatment effects over time; (5) new DiD estimators — Callaway-Sant'Anna (2021), Sun-Abraham (2021), Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess (2024), imputation estimators, when and why to use each; (6) DiD applications in health economics — Medicaid expansion studies (Sommers et al., Courtemanche et al.), ACA provision evaluations, hospital merger effects, payment reform evaluations; (7) triple differences (DDD) — when single DiD fails, adding a within-group comparison, applications and examples; (8) synthetic control method — Abadie-Diamond-Hainmueller (2010, 2015) framework, construction of synthetic counterfactual, inference via permutation (placebo-in-space tests), advantages over DiD for single-treated-unit studies; (9) SCM applications in health economics — state-level policy evaluations, estimating effects of hospital closures on communities; (10) augmented synthetic control (Ben-Michael et al. 2021) and synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021). Include full mathematical derivations and detailed replication discussions of landmark health economics DiD and SCM papers.
context_summary: Chapters 9-10 established econometric foundations and IV methods. This chapter covers the two most widely used quasi-experimental designs for evaluating healthcare policies that roll out across geographic units or time periods.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Regression Discontinuity Design in Health Economics
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on regression discontinuity design (RDD) for graduate health economics researchers. Cover: (1) the sharp RD design — setup, the RD assumption (continuity of potential outcomes at cutoff), local randomization interpretation, graphical analysis at the cutoff; (2) estimation — local linear regression, bandwidth selection (Imbens-Kalyanaraman optimal bandwidth, Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik robust bandwidth), kernel choice, polynomial order selection and the dangers of high-order global polynomials (Gelman-Imbens 2019); (3) the fuzzy RD design — partial compliance at the cutoff, fuzzy RD as IV, estimation of the LATE at the cutoff; (4) validity tests — McCrary density test for manipulation, covariate balance at the cutoff, sensitivity to bandwidth choice, donut-hole RD; (5) RD applications in health economics — Medicare eligibility at age 65 (Card-Dobkin-Maestas 2008, 2009), Medicaid income thresholds, birth weight thresholds for NICU admission (Almond et al. 2010), hospital quality star ratings cutoffs, pay-for-performance threshold effects; (6) multi-cutoff and multi-score RD designs; (7) RD with discrete running variables — the challenge of mass points, approaches from Lee and Card (2008); (8) regression kink design (RKD) — setup, applications in health insurance (kinks in cost-sharing schedules), estimation. Include full mathematical derivations of the sharp and fuzzy RD estimators, bandwidth selection procedures, and detailed walkthroughs of at least two landmark health economics RD papers.
context_summary: Chapters 9-11 covered OLS/GLM, IV methods, and DiD/synthetic control. This chapter completes the quasi-experimental methods toolkit with regression discontinuity designs.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Count Data, Duration Models, and Healthcare Utilization
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on specialized econometric models for healthcare utilization data for graduate researchers. Cover: (1) count data models — Poisson regression (derivation, equidispersion assumption, interpretation of incidence rate ratios), negative binomial regression (NB1 and NB2 parameterizations, overdispersion test), zero-inflated models (ZIP, ZINB), hurdle models; (2) choosing among count models — Cameron-Trivedi tests, Vuong test for zero-inflation; (3) healthcare expenditure models — log-OLS with smearing retransformation (Duan 1983), GLM with log link and gamma family (Manning-Mullahy 2001), the extended estimating equations (EEE) approach; (4) two-part models revisited — first-part as probit/logit, second-part specifications, combining predictions, bootstrap standard errors; (5) survival analysis / duration models — hazard functions, Kaplan-Meier estimation, Cox proportional hazards model (partial likelihood derivation), parametric duration models (exponential, Weibull, log-normal, generalized gamma, Gompertz), accelerated failure time interpretation, competing risks models; (6) recurrent event analysis — Anderson-Gill model, frailty models for unobserved heterogeneity; (7) applications — modeling hospital readmission rates, length of stay analysis, prescription refill patterns. Each model section should include mathematical derivation, log-likelihood specification, interpretation guidance, and a health economics application example.
context_summary: Chapters 9-12 covered causal inference methods (IV, DiD, RD). This chapter addresses the specialized econometric models needed for healthcare's distinctive data types.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Discrete Choice Models in Health Economics
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on discrete choice models for graduate health economics researchers. Cover: (1) random utility theory foundations — utility maximization, the random utility model, IIA property; (2) binary choice models — probit and logit derivation from latent variable framework, marginal effects (at means vs. average marginal effects); (3) multinomial choice — multinomial logit (McFadden 1974), conditional logit, the IIA problem and Hausman-McFadden test; (4) nested logit — tree structure, the dissimilarity parameter, application to hospital choice; (5) mixed logit (random parameters logit) — taste heterogeneity, simulation-based estimation, application to health insurance plan choice (Handel 2013, Ericson-Starc 2015); (6) latent class models — finite mixture approach, class enumeration, application to patient types; (7) ordered choice models — ordered probit/logit for self-reported health status; (8) discrete choice experiments (DCEs) in health economics — experimental design (D-optimal, Bayesian efficient), willingness-to-pay estimation, FDA applications (de Bekker-Grob et al. 2012); (9) structural demand estimation — BLP (Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes 1995) basics applied to hospital and insurance demand; (10) applied examples — hospital choice, insurance plan choice, physician specialty choice. Include mathematical derivations of MLE for each model class.
context_summary: Chapters 9-13 covered linear models, causal inference, count data, and duration models. This chapter addresses discrete choice — the econometric framework for modeling choices among healthcare alternatives.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Bayesian Methods in Health Economics
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on Bayesian statistical methods applied to health economics research for graduate researchers. Cover: (1) Bayesian foundations — Bayes' theorem as update rule, prior-likelihood-posterior framework, conjugate priors, non-informative and weakly informative priors; (2) Bayesian computation — MCMC basics, Gibbs sampling, Metropolis-Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and NUTS, convergence diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample size, trace plots); (3) Bayesian regression models — Bayesian linear regression, Bayesian logistic regression, hierarchical/multilevel models for clustered healthcare data; (4) Bayesian network meta-analysis — the NMA framework, consistency and inconsistency models, ranking treatments (SUCRA); (5) Bayesian cost-effectiveness analysis — joint posterior distribution of costs and effects, cost-effectiveness acceptability curves from posterior simulation, value of information analysis (EVPI, EVPPI); (6) Bayesian decision-analytic models — Markov models with Bayesian parameter estimation, PSA as posterior predictive exercise; (7) Bayesian methods for small area estimation — disease mapping, spatial models (BYM model); (8) empirical Bayes methods — shrinkage estimation for hospital profiling, CMS star ratings methodology. Include mathematical derivations of posterior distributions for key models and complete worked examples.
context_summary: Chapters 9-14 covered frequentist econometric methods. This chapter introduces the Bayesian paradigm, increasingly important in health technology assessment, network meta-analysis, and spatial health economics.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Machine Learning Methods for Health Economics Research
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on machine learning methods applied to health economics for graduate researchers. Cover: (1) the prediction-inference distinction — Mullainathan-Spiess (2017); (2) regularization methods — LASSO, Ridge, Elastic Net, cross-validation, post-LASSO for inference; (3) tree-based methods — CART, random forests (Breiman 2001), gradient boosted trees (XGBoost), variable importance, partial dependence plots; (4) causal forests — Athey-Imbens (2016) generalized random forests, CATE estimation, honest estimation; (5) double/debiased machine learning — Chernozhukov et al. (2018) DML framework, sample splitting, cross-fitting; (6) ML for variable selection in causal models — LASSO-based instrument selection, post-double-selection; (7) deep learning basics — neural network architecture, NLP for clinical notes, transfer learning; (8) ML for healthcare operations — demand forecasting, scheduling, capacity planning; (9) ethical considerations — algorithmic fairness, Obermeyer et al. (2019) racial bias; (10) practical guidance — when to use ML vs. traditional econometrics, model validation, reporting standards. Include mathematical derivations of LASSO, causal forests, and the DML estimator.
context_summary: Chapters 9-15 covered traditional econometric and Bayesian methods. This chapter bridges ML and causal inference — the frontier of health economics methodology.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Structural Estimation in Health Economics
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on structural econometric models in health economics for advanced graduate researchers. Cover: (1) reduced-form vs. structural approaches — when structural estimation is worth the additional assumptions; (2) static structural models — discrete choice demand estimation (BLP for hospital and insurance markets), supply-side models of provider behavior, equilibrium models of insurer-provider bargaining (Ho-Lee 2017, Gowrisankaran-Nevo-Town 2015); (3) dynamic structural models — dynamic discrete choice (Rust 1987 framework), solution methods (backward induction, CCP estimation), application to technology adoption and medication adherence; (4) dynamic programming and health — the Grossman model as dynamic optimization, numerical solution methods; (5) equilibrium models of insurance markets — Einav-Finkelstein-Cullen (2010), adverse selection welfare analysis, mandate vs. penalty analysis; (6) bargaining models — Nash bargaining in hospital-insurer negotiations, merger simulation; (7) structural models of physician behavior — agency models, effort supply under different payment contracts; (8) computational methods — NFXP, MPEC, simulation-based estimation, GMM. Include mathematical derivations of key structural models and discussion of identification strategies.
context_summary: Chapters 9-16 covered reduced-form econometrics, Bayesian methods, and ML. This chapter introduces structural estimation — the most theoretically demanding approach in health economics.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Healthcare Data Sources and Research Design
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter for graduate health economics researchers on major US healthcare datasets and research design considerations. Cover: (1) claims-based datasets — Medicare claims (MedPAR, Carrier, Outpatient, Part D Event files), CMS ResDAC access; Medicaid MAX/T-MSIS; MarketScan; FAIR Health; APCDs; (2) survey datasets — MEPS (overlapping panel design, expenditure estimation), NHIS, BRFSS, CPS, ACS, HRS; (3) clinical/EHR data — PCORnet, TriNetX, Optum/Clinformatics, NLP applications, data quality issues; (4) hospital-level data — AHA Annual Survey, CMS Hospital Cost Reports (HCRIS), Dartmouth Atlas, CMS Hospital Compare/HCAHPS; (5) provider-level data — NPPES, Medicare Provider Utilization files, Physician Compare; (6) area-level data — AHRF, Census/ACS, USDA RUCA codes, CDC WONDER; (7) linkage strategies — claims to EHR, geographic linkage (ZIP-ZCTA crosswalks), NDI mortality linkage; (8) research design considerations — retrospective cohort construction from claims, defining exposure variables, outcome measurement algorithms (sensitivity/specificity), washout periods, lookback windows; (9) data quality — coding accuracy, ICD-9 to ICD-10 transition, misclassification bias, informative censoring. Provide practical guidance a researcher would need to design and execute a claims-based health economics study.
context_summary: Chapters 1-17 covered theory and methods. This chapter is the practical bridge — the actual datasets and research design patterns that health economists use.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Introduction to Julia for Health Economics Research
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter introducing the Julia programming language to health economics researchers who may have experience with Stata, R, or Python. Cover: (1) why Julia for health economics — the two-language problem, JIT compilation, benchmark comparisons; (2) Julia language fundamentals — types, multiple dispatch, functions, arrays, strings, dictionaries; (3) Julia's type system — parametric types, type stability, @code_warntype; (4) control flow and iteration — loops (fast in Julia!), comprehensions, map/filter/reduce; (5) modules and packages — Pkg environment system, Project.toml and Manifest.toml; (6) key ecosystem packages — DataFrames.jl, CSV.jl, GLM.jl, FixedEffectModels.jl, Survival.jl, Distributions.jl, Optim.jl, Turing.jl, MLJ.jl, Plots.jl/Makie.jl; (7) performance engineering — BenchmarkTools, profiling, type stability, memory allocation; (8) Julia vs. Stata/R/Python comparison — syntax mapping tables, migration guide. Include extensive code examples and a complete worked example.
context_summary: Chapters 1-18 covered health economics theory, methods, and data sources. This chapter begins the computational implementation section.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Data Management and Wrangling for Healthcare Data in Julia
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on healthcare data management using Julia for graduate researchers. Cover: (1) DataFrames.jl fundamentals — creating, indexing, subsetting, DataFramesMeta.jl macros (@select, @transform, @subset, @orderby, @combine); (2) reading healthcare data — CSV.jl (chunked reading for large Medicare files), Arrow.jl (columnar storage), XLSX.jl, SASLib.jl; (3) data cleaning — missing values (Julia's missing type, skipmissing, coalesce), ICD code parsing, date/time handling; (4) merging and joining — join types, claims-to-enrollment merges, geographic linkage (ZIP-ZCTA crosswalks); (5) reshaping and aggregation — long-to-wide, groupby-combine for patient-level summaries, episode-of-care construction; (6) medical code systems — ICD-9/ICD-10 lookup tables, CCS/CCSR mapping, implementing Elixhauser and Charlson comorbidity algorithms; (7) large dataset strategies — Arrow memory mapping, database integration (LibPQ.jl, SQLite.jl), parallel data processing; (8) data validation — assertion-based pipelines, duplicate detection, referential integrity checks. Include complete code examples with realistic healthcare data scenarios.
context_summary: Chapter 19 introduced Julia fundamentals. This chapter covers the data management operations that consume 60-80% of a health economist's time.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Statistical Computing and Regression in Julia
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter implementing the core econometric methods from Chapters 9-13 in Julia. Cover: (1) OLS regression — GLM.jl @formula interface, robust standard errors (CovarianceMatrices.jl), clustered standard errors; (2) fixed effects models — FixedEffectModels.jl for high-dimensional fixed effects, fe() notation; (3) instrumental variables — 2SLS in Julia, first-stage diagnostics, weak instrument tests; (4) GLM for healthcare costs — log link and Gamma family, modified Park test implementation; (5) count data models — Poisson and Negative Binomial, zero-inflated models; (6) binary choice and discrete choice — logistic regression, marginal effects computation; (7) two-part models — implementation with bootstrap inference; (8) survival analysis — Survival.jl for Kaplan-Meier and Cox PH, parametric survival; (9) difference-in-differences — event study plots, Callaway-Sant'Anna estimator; (10) regression diagnostics — residual analysis, VIF, specification tests; (11) presenting results — publication-quality regression tables and coefficient plots. Every section should include complete, runnable Julia code with simulated healthcare data examples.
context_summary: Chapters 19-20 covered Julia fundamentals and data wrangling. This chapter implements the econometric methods from the methodology chapters in Julia.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Bayesian Computation in Julia with Turing.jl
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on Bayesian computation in Julia using Turing.jl. Cover: (1) Turing.jl architecture — the @model macro, ~ notation, automatic differentiation; (2) Bayesian regression models — linear, logistic, hierarchical models for provider-level data; (3) prior specification for health economics — priors for treatment effects, cost parameters, utility weights; (4) MCMC sampling — NUTS configuration, chain diagnostics, thinning, warmup, multiple chains; (5) Bayesian hierarchical models — hospital quality estimation with shrinkage, patient outcomes nested within providers; (6) Bayesian CEA — joint cost-effect modeling, CEAC construction, EVPI from posterior draws; (7) Bayesian NMA — fixed and random effects NMA, SUCRA ranking; (8) Bayesian survival models — parametric survival with Turing.jl; (9) model comparison — WAIC, LOO-CV (ParetoSmooth.jl), posterior predictive checks; (10) advanced topics — Gaussian processes, Bayesian structural time series, variational inference. Include complete Turing.jl code for every model.
context_summary: Chapters 19-21 covered Julia fundamentals, data wrangling, and frequentist regression. Chapter 15 covered Bayesian theory. This chapter implements Bayesian methods using Turing.jl.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Simulation and Microsimulation for Health Economics in Julia
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on building simulation models for health economic evaluation in Julia. Cover: (1) Monte Carlo simulation fundamentals — random number generation, Distributions.jl, Latin Hypercube Sampling, correlation structure; (2) decision tree models — implementing probabilistic decision trees, expected value calculation, complete CEA decision tree example; (3) Markov cohort models — transition probability matrices, cycle correction, discounting, computing QALYs and costs, complete Markov CEA model; (4) microsimulation — individual-level simulation paradigm, Patient structs, tracking histories, heterogeneous treatment effects, complete microsimulation CEA; (5) discrete event simulation — DES concepts, SimJulia.jl/ConcurrentSim.jl, hospital capacity planning; (6) probabilistic sensitivity analysis — PSA via Monte Carlo draws, CEAC construction, EVPI calculation; (7) model calibration — Optim.jl, Bayesian calibration with Turing.jl; (8) model validation protocols; (9) performance optimization — @threads, CUDA.jl, vectorized simulation. Include complete Julia implementations of decision tree CEA, Markov CEA, and microsimulation with PSA.
context_summary: Chapters 19-22 covered Julia programming and Bayesian methods. Chapter 6 covered CEA theory. This chapter implements simulation methods central to health technology assessment.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Machine Learning Implementation in Julia for Health Economics
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter implementing ML methods for health economics in Julia. Cover: (1) MLJ.jl ecosystem — unified API, model registry, scientific types, pipelines; (2) data preprocessing — feature engineering for claims data, one-hot encoding, temporal train/test splits; (3) regularized regression — LASSO, Ridge, Elastic Net via MLJ.jl, cross-validation tuning; (4) tree-based methods — random forests, gradient boosted trees (EvoTrees.jl), feature importance, SHAP values; (5) causal forests — custom GRF implementation, honest estimation, CATE confidence intervals; (6) double/debiased machine learning — cross-fitting implementation, nuisance function estimation; (7) neural networks — Flux.jl basics for healthcare, tabular deep learning; (8) model evaluation — ROC, calibration, Brier scores, decision curves; (9) fairness auditing — equalized odds, calibration by group, Obermeyer replication; (10) complete ML pipeline — readmission prediction end-to-end. Include complete Julia code for every section.
context_summary: Chapter 16 covered ML theory. Chapters 19-23 covered Julia programming through simulation. This chapter implements ML methods in Julia.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Data Visualization and Scientific Communication in Julia
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on creating publication-quality visualizations for health economics research using Julia. Cover: (1) Julia visualization ecosystem — Plots.jl, Makie.jl (CairoMakie), AlgebraOfGraphics.jl; (2) exploratory data analysis — histograms, KDE plots, box plots for healthcare costs and utilization; (3) regression result visualization — coefficient plots, marginal effects plots; (4) causal inference visualization — event study plots, RD plots with binned scatter and fit; (5) CEA visualization — CE plane, CEAC, tornado diagrams, net benefit plots; (6) geographic visualization — choropleth maps with GeoMakie.jl, point maps; (7) publication formatting — figure sizing, fonts, colorblind-accessible palettes, multi-panel figures; (8) interactive visualization — WGLMakie, PlotlyJS.jl, Pluto.jl; (9) tables — PrettyTables.jl for regression tables, Table 1 format; (10) reproducible figures — figure-generation scripts, multi-format saving. Include complete code for every visualization type.
context_summary: Chapters 19-24 covered Julia computation. This chapter focuses on communicating results visually through publication-quality figures and tables.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Building Reproducible Research Pipelines in Julia
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on creating reproducible health economics research pipelines in Julia. Cover: (1) reproducibility importance — replication failures, journal requirements; (2) Julia project management — Project.toml, Manifest.toml, environment isolation; (3) literate programming — Pluto.jl reactive notebooks, Quarto with Julia, Weave.jl; (4) data pipeline architecture — DrWatson.jl for scientific project management, naming conventions; (5) testing research code — Test standard library, testing against analytical solutions, regression tests, CI with GitHub Actions; (6) version control — Git workflow, branching, Git LFS for data, DVC; (7) automation — Makefile-style build systems, incremental rebuilding; (8) documentation — Documenter.jl, README templates, data dictionaries; (9) performance and scaling — Profile, parallel processing, Distributed standard library; (10) packaging research as Julia package — General registry; (11) archival — Zenodo, Docker, Binder. Include a complete worked example of setting up a health economics research project.
context_summary: Chapters 19-25 covered Julia implementation of all methods. This chapter addresses software engineering practices for reproducible research.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Building a Complete Health Economics Analysis: An Integrated Case Study
prompt: Write a comprehensive capstone chapter walking through a complete health economics research project from conception to manuscript-ready results. The case study analyzes the effect of Medicaid expansion on hospital financial performance and quality outcomes using a staggered difference-in-differences design. Cover: (1) research question formulation — translating policy question into testable specification; (2) data assembly in Julia — loading and merging CMS HCRIS, AHA Annual Survey, CMS Hospital Compare, and Census/ACS data; (3) descriptive analysis — Table 1, pre-trend visualizations; (4) econometric specification — staggered DiD with Callaway-Sant'Anna, event study, state-clustered SEs; (5) implementation in Julia — FixedEffectModels.jl, custom CS estimator, Makie.jl plots; (6) robustness checks — alternative specifications, placebo tests, synthetic control for individual states; (7) heterogeneity analysis — differential effects by hospital type, causal forests for CATE; (8) CEA extension — Markov model for cost-effectiveness of expansion; (9) manuscript preparation — generating all tables, figures, and replication package. This chapter ties together theory (1-8), methods (9-17), data (18), and Julia implementation (19-26).
context_summary: This is the capstone chapter integrating all 26 prior chapters into a complete research project.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Advanced Topics: Spatial Health Economics and Geographic Variation
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on spatial and geographic methods in health economics with Julia implementations. Cover: (1) the Dartmouth Atlas and geographic variation — Wennberg's foundational research, supply-sensitive vs. preference-sensitive vs. effective care; (2) spatial econometrics — spatial weight matrices (contiguity, distance-based, k-nearest neighbors), spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I, Geary's C), spatial lag and spatial error models, spatial Durbin model; (3) implementing spatial econometrics in Julia — constructing weight matrices from shapefiles, spatial regression, interpreting direct and indirect effects; (4) geographic access to care — Euclidean distance, travel time, two-step floating catchment area (2SFCA) method; (5) spatial models for health outcomes — disease mapping with spatial smoothing, Bayesian BYM model in Turing.jl, cluster detection; (6) geographic variation in spending — decomposing price vs. quantity, supply-side vs. demand-side explanations; (7) hospital market definition — Elzinga-Hogarty test, variable radius methods, CMS market definitions; (8) the Finkelstein-Gentzkow-Williams (2016) movers design — decomposing variation into demand and supply components. Include Julia code for spatial weight matrices, spatial regressions, choropleth maps, and 2SFCA method.
context_summary: Chapters 1-27 covered core theory, methods, and Julia implementation including a capstone case study. This chapter addresses spatial methods for geographic variation research.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: Advanced Topics: Dynamic Models, Optimal Policy, and Mechanism Design
prompt: Write a comprehensive chapter on advanced theoretical and computational topics for graduate health economics researchers. Cover: (1) dynamic optimization — the Grossman model as optimal control problem, Bellman equation formulation, value function iteration in Julia; (2) optimal health insurance design — Feldstein (1973) moral hazard welfare loss, optimal cost-sharing with heterogeneous agents, mechanism design for insurance markets; (3) dynamic treatment regimes — sequential decision problems, Q-learning and A-learning for optimal treatment strategies; (4) optimal payment design — mechanism design for provider payment, multitasking and gaming (Holmstrom-Milgrom), computational implementation; (5) dynamic discrete choice models — Rust (1987) framework applied to physician decisions, patient medication adherence, hospital technology adoption, CCP estimation; (6) general equilibrium effects — CGE models for healthcare reform, labor market effects of ESI; (7) optimal experimentation — Bayesian adaptive trial design, Thompson sampling, multi-armed bandits; (8) healthcare market design — matching markets for organ allocation and medical residencies (Roth 2002), auction design for Medicare Advantage. Include mathematical derivations and Julia implementations for value function iteration, Q-learning, and dynamic discrete choice.
context_summary: Chapters 1-28 covered core and spatial health economics. This chapter addresses the most theoretically advanced topics — dynamic optimization, mechanism design, and optimal policy.

textbook_title: Healthcare Economics Research: Methodology and Computational Methods in Julia
title: The Future of Health Economics: Emerging Methods and Frontiers
prompt: Write a comprehensive concluding chapter surveying emerging frontiers of health economics research. Cover: (1) large language models and NLP for health economics — extracting information from clinical notes, automated coding, systematic review automation; (2) causal inference frontiers — synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021), matrix completion, distributional treatment effects, mediation analysis; (3) precision medicine economics — heterogeneous treatment effects, biomarker-based subgroup analysis, pharmacogenomics value; (4) real-world evidence — FDA framework, emulated target trials (Hernan-Robins); (5) digital health economics — wearable devices, remote monitoring, digital therapeutics valuation; (6) climate change and health economics — heat-mortality valuation, air quality health costs, healthcare system resilience; (7) infectious disease economics — SIR/SEIR models with economic extensions, pandemic preparedness value, COVID-19 methodological lessons; (8) behavioral health economics frontiers — commitment devices, social network effects, identity economics; (9) equity and distributional analysis — extended cost-effectiveness analysis (ECEA), concentration indices, health opportunity costs; (10) the Julia ecosystem roadmap — upcoming packages, growing role in scientific computing. Frame each frontier with key references, open research questions, and Julia implementation opportunities.
context_summary: This final chapter surveys research frontiers building on the entire textbook. It should inspire readers to identify their own research contributions.
